analysis.one_liner: Ends the public-interest review required before US natural gas can be exported overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in committee without ever getting a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal parts of the Natural Gas Act that require the federal government to find that exporting or importing natural gas is in the public interest, and that tie export approvals to countries the US has free trade agreements with. It would also give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) sole authority over building, expanding, or operating LNG terminals, including export facilities. The practical effect: natural gas companies could ship gas abroad without a federal review of whether that raises prices or shortchanges American consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas producers and LNG export companies, which could win approval to ship more gas overseas faster, without a public-interest review that weighs effects on domestic prices and supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Natural gas producers and LNG exporters

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that FERC authorize exports or imports of natural gas only if it finds the transaction is in the public interest, and removes restrictions tied to free trade agreements.

Gives FERC exclusive authority to approve or deny applications to site, build, expand, or operate facilities that import or export natural gas, including LNG terminals, making export facility permitting a single-track process.
Preserves the President's separate authority to block exports to sanctioned countries or state sponsors of terrorism under existing sanctions laws.

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses that use natural gas for heating, electricity, and manufacturing. Less gas kept home means more competition for domestic supply, and the public-interest review that used to weigh those costs would no longer apply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Domestic gas users facing higher prices

drawbacks.text: Removing the public-interest test means exports no longer have to be weighed against their effect on domestic prices and supply, so gas shipped abroad could raise heating and electricity costs at home; an honest supporter would acknowledge this trade-off and argue it is offset by trade and energy-security gains.

Concentrating terminal approval authority in FERC alone removes one of the overlapping checks on where and how LNG facilities get built, though supporters argue this speeds permitting for needed export capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows mainly to gas producers and exporters, who gain a faster, lighter-touch path to sell US gas abroad. The cost is borne by domestic gas consumers, who lose the federal review that considered whether exports inflate their prices. There is a real argument on the other side — US LNG helped European allies after Russia's invasion of Ukraine — but the bill as written removes the balancing test entirely rather than refining it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and neither ever considered it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Johnson of Ohio introduced the bill on January 31, 2023, and no other member signed on as a cosponsor.

The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on February 10, 2023, to its Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without a committee vote, a floor vote, or action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, households and businesses that heat homes and power factories with natural gas kept the existing public-interest review on exports. The status quo — which requires the government to weigh domestic consumer effects before approving exports — stayed in place. The bill's intended beneficiaries, gas exporters, gained nothing this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Bill Johnson
for.role: U.S. Representative from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no cosponsors joined.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over natural gas legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill stayed in subcommittee for the full two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of where either party stood beyond the single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and LNG export companies
industries.note: The bill would let them ship more gas abroad without the public-interest review that weighs effects on domestic supply and prices, speeding approvals and expanding their export business. Its gain comes directly at the expense of domestic consumers competing for the same gas.

industries.industry: Domestic natural gas consumers (households, electric utilities, and gas-dependent manufacturers)
industries.note: Removing the public-interest test means exports no longer have to be balanced against domestic price and supply effects, and gas kept home would face more competition from foreign buyers. These consumers are better off that the bill died.
